description: Engineering student working on satellite data integration and local agricultural climate tools.
summary:
Repelón Risk Lens is an open-source research prototype that uses Earth observation data to explore environmental vulnerability and agricultural water needs in Repelón, Colombia.

We developed an interactive tool that screens 1,848 cadastral parcels using CHIRPS rainfall and Sentinel-2 vegetation indicators. A complementary model uses NASA POWER meteorological data and FAO-56 methods to estimate crop-water shortfalls across six crops, twelve planting months, and three hypothetical crop rotations. NASA GPM IMERG provides an additional rainfall comparison.

Our project addresses the challenge by transforming complex environmental datasets into understandable maps, indicators, and agricultural scenarios that can support further investigation.

Its greatest strength is transparency. We discovered that changing the rainfall dataset substantially alters risk classifications, demonstrating why uncertainty must be communicated rather than hidden. We also distinguish environmental screening from actual crop losses and modeled water deficits from verified agricultural outcomes.

Repelón Risk Lens does not claim to predict harvests or prescribe planting decisions. Instead, it provides an explainable, reproducible foundation for exploring agricultural adaptation strategies and identifying where local validation is needed.
details:
What we developed

Repelón Risk Lens is an open-source, interactive research prototype designed to explore environmental vulnerability and agricultural water requirements in Repelón, Atlántico, Colombia. It combines satellite observations, meteorological data, cadastral boundaries, and transparent mathematical models to help users investigate agricultural conditions and compare hypothetical adaptation scenarios.

Rather than attempting to predict crop failures or automatically prescribe planting strategies, the project focuses on making environmental information accessible, explainable, and reproducible.

How it works

The project consists of two complementary analytical components.

1. Parcel-level environmental screening

We analyzed 1,848 unique cadastral parcels using precipitation data from CHIRPS and vegetation indicators derived from ESA Sentinel-2 imagery, including NDVI, NDMI, and SAVI.

A transparent, rule-based model combines normalized rainfall hazard and vegetation vulnerability into an environmental screening index. The results are displayed through an interactive map where users can explore parcel characteristics, environmental indicators, and rainfall sensitivity.

The screening classified 858 parcels as Low, 579 as Moderate, and 411 as High. However, our analysis revealed that 406 of the 411 High-classified parcels are smaller than 0.1 hectares, and only 10 are predominantly agricultural.

This distinction is essential: a high environmental screening score does not necessarily indicate agricultural damage or crop failure.

2. Crop-water and rotation exploration

Using daily meteorological data from NASA POWER, we implemented the FAO-56 Penman–Monteith methodology to estimate reference evapotranspiration (ET0).

Crop evapotranspiration (ETc) is estimated using literature-based crop coefficients (Kc), while climatic water shortfall is calculated by comparing crop water requirements against precipitation.

We explored six crops: maize, sorghum, cassava, dry beans, tomato, and rice.

The analysis includes 1,662 crop-cycle simulations across different planting conditions and three hypothetical crop-rotation sequences evaluated over a 24-month horizon.

These scenarios allow users to compare how planting month, crop selection, and rotation structure influence modeled water requirements. They are exploratory comparisons rather than validated recommendations for individual farms.

Why NASA data matters

NASA POWER provides the daily meteorological variables needed to estimate atmospheric water demand and evaluate crop-water scenarios. Without these data, the project would lack its quantitative foundation for comparing agricultural water requirements across planting periods.

NASA GPM IMERG was also used as an alternative precipitation source to examine the sensitivity of the environmental screening model.

One of our most important findings was that the same screening methodology produced 411 High-classified parcels using CHIRPS but only 38 using GPM.

Rather than concealing this disagreement, we documented it to demonstrate how strongly environmental classifications can depend on data-source selection.

Technology and development

The project was developed using Python for geospatial processing, environmental calculations, and exploratory analysis, alongside Google Colab and Google Earth Engine for working with satellite and meteorological datasets.

The interactive web application uses JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with Leaflet for geographic visualization.

Additional resources include ESA WorldCover land-cover information, SoilGrids soil data, Colombian cadastral information, municipal agricultural statistics, and a preliminary comparison with IDEAM rainfall observations.

The methodology, assumptions, limitations, and reproducibility materials are documented in the public GitHub repository. AI-assisted tools were used to support programming, debugging, documentation, and visual communication; the underlying observational datasets were obtained from their original sources.

No specialized physical hardware was required.

Creativity and intended impact

The project's main innovation is not a complex predictive algorithm, but the integration of environmental screening, crop-water modeling, and explicit uncertainty communication within an accessible research tool.

We deliberately prioritized explainable calculations over black-box predictions.

Our analysis also exposed important methodological limitations, including sensitivity to precipitation datasets, differences in parcel size and land cover, uncertainty in literature-based crop coefficients, and the absence of local field validation.

These limitations are presented openly because we believe responsible agricultural decision-support tools should communicate not only what their models calculate, but also what those calculations cannot establish.

Repelón Risk Lens aims to provide a reproducible foundation for future agricultural adaptation research, encourage critical interpretation of Earth observation data, and help identify where local measurements and field validation would be most valuable.

Our guiding principle is simple: Repelón Risk Lens doesn't hide uncertainty. It makes uncertainty visible.
